signals.headline: Liability benchmark rises £30.1m over four years (£123.7m → £153.8m); Table 1 residual line flips from +£17.5m surplus to -£31.3m new borrowing by 31.3.29, driven by an HRA CFR that grows £19.8m
signals.why_it_matters: The strategy plan itself embeds new borrowing of around £31m over four years, arriving into a market whose PWLB certainty curve is currently 5.34%–6.46% against a budget assumption of 5.1%.

signals.headline: Clean forward-looking strategy: 100% PWLB external debt, no LOBO, no market debt, no pooled funds, no commercial exposure, all prudential indicators within strategic limits
signals.why_it_matters: A defensively positioned district, and a paper that reads honestly (explicit cost-of-carry framing, verbatim conflict-of-interest exclusion). Reading it and finding nothing alarming is a real product output.

summary.text:
Chesterfield's 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy is a short covering report plus a twelve-page Appendix A that went to both Council and Standards and Audit on 25 February 2026. Simple book: £122.2m of external borrowing all in PWLB at a weighted 3.6% (31 December 2025), and £16.4m of treasury investments split £1.5m Government and £14.9m Money Market Funds at 3.9% weighted. No LOBO, no pooled funds, no property, no commercial-investment exposure. Total CFR £190.4m at 31.3.25 (GF £57.4m + HRA £133.0m) forecast to rise to £209.0m by 31.3.29, all of the growth in the HRA CFR (+£19.8m). Internal borrowing rises £58.4m → £96.5m over four years as the council pursues the stated strategy of holding external borrowing and investments below their underlying levels. Liability benchmark climbs £30m over four years to £153.8m at 31.3.29 while forecast external borrowing runs off to £112.5m — Table 1's last row states the residual: £31.3m of new borrowing implied by 31.3.29.

The loan book reconciles neatly. Our current live file carries 80 PWLB loans at £120,613,002, weighted 3.52%. That matches the paper's own 31.3.26 estimate of £120.6m to the pound, and sits £1.6m and 0.08 points off the printed 31.12.25 actual (£122.2m at 3.6%) — a movement consistent with normal annuity paydown over eight months. The balance-sheet identity — CFR minus external borrowing minus other long-term liabilities equals internal borrowing — holds on all five columns of Table 1 (31.3.25 actual through 31.3.29 forecast) to the £0.1m the table is rounded to. Safe to cite either.

The hook worth writing is the 5.1% average rate the paper assumes for new long-term borrowing in 2026/27 (Financial Implications, page 11), paired with Arlingclose's Bank Rate forecast (dated 22 December 2025) that Bank Rate reaches around 3.25% in 2026. Today's PWLB certainty curve at notice 314/26 PM is 5.34% at 5 years, 5.83% at 10, 6.46% at 25 and 6.27% at 50 — all above the 5.1% assumption. Bank Rate is still 3.75%, and SONIA is pricing one-year Bank Rate at 4.11%, not 3.25%. The paper itself explicitly acknowledges the cost-of-carry vs breakeven decision that this raises (§Borrowing Strategy, page 4). Not a criticism — a testable statement whose anchor has moved eight months on, on which we happen to publish daily. Email drafted; ready to send to the report author Theresa Channell whose email is published on page 7 of the covering report. Her title is not stated; the paper's Financial Implications section refers to the S151 role as 'the Service Director - Finance' (unnamed) and the Related Matters section refers to 'the Chief Finance Officer' (also unnamed).

officer.subject: Your 5.1% new-borrowing rate for 2026/27, against today's PWLB curve
officer.body:
Hi Theresa,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the 2026/27 Strategy that went to Council on 25 February, offered in the spirit of a paper that reads carefully and doesn't overreach. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. We hold 80 live PWLB loans for Chesterfield totalling £120.6m at a weighted 3.52%, against your page 11 print of £122.2m at 3.6% on 31 December 2025. The gap is £1.6m and eight-hundredths of a point — small annuity paydown over eight months — and our current live figure lands within a pound of your Table 1 estimate for 31 March 2026 (£120.6m). While we were in the paper we also ran the balance-sheet identity across Table 1 (CFR minus external borrowing minus other long-term liabilities equals internal borrowing): it holds cleanly on all five columns from 31.3.25 actual through to 31.3.29 forecast, to the £0.1m the table itself is rounded to. So everything below is written against a book we can see clearly.

The reason we wrote is the 5.1% average rate you've assumed for new long-term borrowing in 2026/27 (Financial Implications, page 11), together with the Arlingclose forecast that Bank Rate reaches around 3.25% in 2026 (page 2, dated 22 December). Both are testable statements. At the daily 314/26 PM fixing this afternoon, PWLB certainty maturity rates are 5.34% at five years, 5.83% at ten, 6.46% at twenty-five and 6.27% at fifty — every point above the 5.1% assumption, so the 5.1% would only be reachable at the short end today. Bank Rate is still 3.75%, and SONIA is pricing one-year Bank Rate closer to 4.11%, not 3.25%. That doesn't make the strategy wrong; your own Borrowing Strategy section is explicit that cost-of-carry and breakeven analysis may push you to borrow long anyway, "even if this causes additional cost in the short-term". But the anchor the December forecast set has moved. The place to keep an eye on both fixings and the SONIA path is pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, which also publishes every PWLB loan the sector draws each month.

The other side of that question is size. The last row of your Table 1 flips from a £17.5m treasury investment surplus at 31.3.25 to £31.3m of implied new borrowing by 31.3.29. Table 2's liability benchmark tells the same story from a different angle, rising from £123.7m to £153.8m over the same four years while forecast external borrowing runs off to £112.5m. About £31m of new external raised in a curve of the shape today's would compound the question in the paragraph above; split into short-dated rolls it would move the interest-rate exposure indicator on page 9 (you've set £300k on a 1% rise, £400k on a 1% fall). An interactive version of the liability benchmark — CIPFA has put it closer to centre stage in the code updates — is at pwlbtoday.org/liability-benchmark and rebuilds live off the curve.

Your own book, priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. Break costs are indicative only — only the DMO can give a binding quote, and we model no MRP or accounting treatment.

On training, three fit Chesterfield well. Strategic PWLB borrowing sits behind the 5.1% question and the cost-of-carry framework the paper flags. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice goes to the £30m rise in Table 2 and how to translate it into a phasing plan. And Rate risk goes straight to page 9's interest-rate exposure indicators — translating the £300k/£400k ceilings into the sensitivity of the whole £120m book is what the course does. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
